docs.title: QGIS TUFLOW Plugin Documentation
docs.text:
Welcome to the QGIS TUFLOW Plugin documentation!

This page provides an ever growing list of documentation pages that are being moved from the TUFLOW Wiki onto a more modern platform.

Currently, the majority of documentation is still provided on the TUFLOW Wiki which is not planned to be removed. However, as tools continue to develop, their documentation may be moved onto this platform and the wiki pages will become superseded. Notices will be added to those wiki pages when this happens.

docs.title: ARR to TUFLOW
docs.text:
Experimental

This tool is labelled experimental. Outputs should be checked carefully.

The layout and functionality of the tool may change in a future version without providing backward compatibility to prior functionality.

Feedback is welcome. During the initial phases of the tool's release, feedback will greatly influence the functionality and look of this new version of the tool. Contact support@tuflow.com with any feedback.

The ARR to TUFLOW tool converts Australian Rainfall and Runoff rainfall and loss data from the ARR Data Hub into TUFLOW model input files (Event_File.tef, bc_dbase.csv, rf_inflow/*.csv, .tsoilf).

This tool is a clean rewrite of the ARR to TUFLOW tool, now referred to as the ARR to TUFLOW (legacy) tool. The rewrite allows the legacy tool to co-exist, enabling backward compatibility and an easy access point to the legacy ARR Data Hub. This also allows the replication of outputs from the tool prior to the 2026 v1 ARR Data Hub update.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
The ARR to TUFLOW tool can be opened by clicking the icon in the plugin toolbar.

The new tool and legacy tool share the same toolbar spot

Use the drop down arrow to switch between the new and legacy ARR to TUFLOW tools.

The ARR to TUFLOW tool window is split into several tabs for different setting groups. At its simplest, only the Required Settings tab needs to be reviewed and all other tabs can be left as default, noting that defaults aren't necessarily going to be best for all catchments or in perpetuity.

Below is a basic workflow to run the tool. For further details on the inputs, refer to the Configuration Options section of the documentation.

  1. Load a catchment GIS polygon file into QGIS.
  2. Select the catchment layer in the Populate table from layer combobox and the select the naming field in the Catchment identifier field combobox.

  3. Click to populate the catchment table with the catchment.

  4. Select an output location for the TUFLOW files.

  5. Select at least one AEP and one duration event.

  6. Click Run and wait for the tool to finish.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
The tool outputs (with the exception of the working_data outputs) are identical to the legacy tool. The following example on the TUFLOW Wiki shows the outputs and how they can be used in a TUFLOW model:

wiki.tuflow.com/QGIS_ARR_to_TUFLOW_Example

docs.title: Log
docs.text:
Logged messages are written to the Log widget at the very bottom of the tool. Messages will not be cleared when the tool is run, and new messages will be appended at the bottom after messages from any previous runs. Messages will not be saved between QGIS sessions and the log widget will be cleared if QGIS is closed.

If an error occurs, the log widget will automatically expand showing the error message. It is also considered good practice to open the log widget, even after a successful run, to check for warning messages.

Messages produced by the interface are also written here. Checking the log widget for any messages is a good place to start when troubleshooting any aspect of the tool.

docs.title: Areal Reduction Factor (ARF)
docs.text:
The tool will automatically apply ARF values to the rainfall depths in the outputs. For example, the inflow data in the rf_inflow/*.csv outputs are already ARF adjusted.

The applied ARF is based on the catchment area and other settings described below.

docs.title: Catchment Area
docs.text:
This option sets the catchment area which is used to determine the ARF value and whether to use point or areal temporal patterns.

The catchment area can set using either:

  • Calculate area (default): Let the tool calculate the area using the polygon geometry.

  • User area: Manually set the catchment area (km2).

    This method can be useful when looping through subcatchments. The user can set the total catchment area rather than letting each subcatchment compute an independent ARF for each subcatchment.

    The ARR guidelines recommend that the ARF should be computed for the upstream area at each point of interest, but not independently for each subarea (Book 2, Chapter 4, Section 3.1).

docs.title: ARF Settings
docs.text:
There are several other ARF settings which are described below:

  • Minimum ARF value Sets a floor to the calculated ARF. This must be a value between 0 and 1.

  • ARF for events < 50% AEP Events less than the 50% AEP are outside the guidance for the given ARF equations in the ARR guidelines. If this option is checked on, the tool will ignore the limit and calculate the ARF for frequent events. If unchecked, an ARF value of one (1.0) will be used.

    Checking this option can be useful to retain continuity in rainfall depths. For example, the 63.2% AEP event might end up with more rainfall (or similar rainfall) than the 50% AEP due to the ARF values (or lack of ARF for the 63.2% AEP event).

  • User override - manually specify ARF Set the ARF that will be used. This will cause the catchment area parameter to be ignored for the ARF.

    Only a single value can be used for all events.

    Catchment area is still used for temporal patterns

    The catchment area is still an important attribute for determining whether to use areal or point temporal patterns.

docs.title: Working Data
docs.text: Calculated ARF values are output into the working_data folder. The working_data ARF values will always be from the calculated ARF using the input catchment area, even if the user specifies an override ARF.

docs.title: Climate Change Scenarios
docs.text:
Climate change scenarios can be added or removed from the table using the corresponding buttons: /

For each row in the Climate change list, the user can select a combination of projection year and Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) scenario.

Each row will have a corresponding row in the Climate change scenario names list, which assigns each scenario a unique name that will correspond to the event/scenario name in the TUFLOW outputs.

docs.title: Initial Loss
docs.text:
Note on complete storm events

If the event is using a complete storm event (preburst + burst), the climate change initial loss is always calculated using the storm initial loss and the climate change factor regardless of the selected option below.

\[ IL_{CC\_storm} = IL_{storm} \times IL_{CC\_factor} \]

There are two options on how to factor the climate change initial loss values:

  1. Scale storm IL (default): The storm method scales the storm initial loss and subtracts the climate change adjusted preburst depth to calculate the burst initial loss.

    \[ IL_{CC\_burst} = IL_{storm} \times IL_{CC\_factor} - PB_{ratio} \times RF_{CC} \]

  2. Scale burst IL: The burst method scales the calculated burst initial loss.

    \[ IL_{CC\_burst} = IL_{burst} \times IL_{CC\_factor} \]

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
By adding climate change scenarios, the following outputs will be turned on:

  • An additional boundary database file: bc_dbase_CC.csv

  • Climate change rainfall boundaries will be added to each event in the rf_inflow/*.csv outputs.

    Climate change TP column names

    Column names within the rainfall boundary files will be suffixed with the unique climate change scenario name.

  • An additional climate change section will be added the event file output (.tef). Each climate change scenario will be listed here using the scenario name.

docs.title: Working Data
docs.text: Adjusted IFD curves and initial loss values for each climate change scenario are output to the working_data folder.

docs.title: Burst Initial Loss Method
docs.text:
This option sets which initial loss table is retrieved from the Data Hub for design burst events:

  • Recommended (default): use the Data Hub's standard/recommended storm initial loss table and calculate the burst loss:

    \[ IL_{burst} = IL_{storm} - PB_{depth} \]

    For the majority of catchments, the data hub provides a single "Storm Initial Loss" value. Catchments in NSW may retrieve an AEP independent loss table.

  • Probability neutral (legacy) (if available): use the Data Hub's "probability neutral" initial loss table, where available (typically only available for NSW catchments).

docs.title: Short Duration Extrapolation Method
docs.text:
Sets how the burst initial loss is extrapolated for durations shorter than those directly provided by the Data Hub (< 30 minutes). The available methods are:

  • Interpolate to zero: the losses are interpolated using the assumption that at the zero minute duration, the initial loss is zero.
  • Log-interpolate to zero: the same as the Interpolate to zero option but it uses a log scale for duration (uses a boundary value of zero for zero minutes).
  • Interpolate pre-burst: the preburst depths are interpolated using the assumption that at the zero minute duration, the preburst depth is zero.
  • Log-interpolate pre-burst: same as Interpolate pre-burst option but uses a log scale for duration (uses a boundary value of zero for zero minutes).
  • Constant: the burst initial loss is held constant from the nearest table row edge. This matches the method named "Use 60 min loss" in the ARR to TUFLOW (legacy) tool.
  • Constant pre-burst ratio (default): the preburst ratio is held constant from the nearest table row/column edge.
  • Rahman et al. 2002: an equation from a study conducted by Rahman et al 2002 is used.
  • Hill et al. 1996/1998 (requires MAR): an equationfrom a study conducted by Hill et al 1996:1998 is used. This requires the user to set the Mean anuual rainfall (MAR) (mm) input.
  • Static value (requires static loss): the loss value is defined by a user input and will be used for all the extrapolated values. The method requires the user to set the static_loss value.

docs.title: TUFLOW Loss Method
docs.text:
Sets how the initial/continuing loss values are written to the TUFLOW model inputs:

  • Infiltration (soil file): losses are written to a .tsoilf soils file. The infiltration approach does not support automatically setting up impervious losses (impervious areas are landcover, and not a soil type). Fraction impervious can be setup in the materials.csv to account for impervious areas.

  • Rainfall excess (material file): losses are written as a rainfall excess initial/continuing loss to a materials file.

    Optionally, Fixed impervious/urban area initial and continuing losses can also be specified and will write an entry into the materials.csv.

docs.title: User Overrides
docs.text:
The calculated initial loss and/or continuing loss values can be overridden with user-specified values:

  • Initial loss (mm): overrides the Storm Initial Loss with a single user-specified value.

  • Continuing loss (mm/hr): overrides the continuing loss for with a single user-specified value.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
There are 2 output files associated with the loss values, dependent on which TUFLOW Loss Method was used:

  • rainfall_losses.trd / soil_infiltration.trd: these files contain the loss values and sets them to a variable based on the storm event. The files are identical, but the naming convention is based on the chosen TUFLOW Loss Method.
  • soils.tsoilf (if using the Infiltration method): the soil definition file for use in the model.
  • materials.csv (if using the Rainfall excess method): the material file that contains rainfall losses defined.

docs.title: Working data
docs.text: The calculated burst initial loss is output to the working_data folder. The placeholder "Use PB TP" (use preburst temporal pattern) is used if a complete storm is triggered (burst initial loss is no longer used).

docs.title: Other Notes / Assumptions
docs.text:
• For missing internal values, the burst initial loss is calculated by interpolating the rainfall and preburst ratios separately and calculating the preburst depth (rather than interpolating the preburst depths directly). Rainfall depths are not always required to be interpolated since there is more event information provided, but if it is interpolated it is done so using linear interpolation in log-log space. Preburst ratios uses linear interpolation in log-linear space (duration and AEP use log space, the preburst value uses linear space).
  • For missing external values, the values are extrapolated by holding the preburst ratio from the nearest column/row edge constant. The exception is for short duration extrapolation, which uses the Short Duration Extrapolation Method setting.
  • For complete storms, the Storm Initial Loss value is always used (either from the data hub or the user specified value).

docs.title: Legacy Data Hub
docs.text:
The legacy Data Hub is only accessible via the ARR to TUFLOW (legacy) tool.

The 2026 v1 update of the Data Hub acts as a boundary between the new and old tools. The legacy tool  works for the legacy Data Hub, but not the 2026 v1 update. The new tool  only works for the 2026 v1 update (and later).

docs.title: Differences with the Legacy Tool
docs.text:
Note

The TUFLOW output format from the tool remains consistent with the ARR to TUFLOW (legacy) tool.

For an example on how to use the outputs in a TUFLOW model setup, please refer to the following TUFLOW Wiki page: wiki.tuflow.com/QGIS_ARR_to_TUFLOW_Example

  • Defaults have changed where appropriate for the 2026 v1 update. For example, the "current" 2030 baseline rainfall year is the default. Other regional/jurisdication specifics such as using the new NSW storm losses (as opposed the the probability neutral losses) is now also the default.

  • The Data Hub API now supports uploading catchment files. Previously, this was not possible and the catchment centroid was used. Now the catchment will be uploaded directly if a GIS layer is provided.

    Warning

    It is the users responsibility to supply a valid catchment polygon. There could be circumstances where the polygon is rejected by the Data Hub e.g. if there are too many vertices or the catchment is not in Australia.

  • The tool does not scrape the BOM website and relies on rainfall depths provided by the Data Hub. Currently, frequent rainfall depths are not provided and as such, frequent events are not yet supported.

  • Preburst rainfall extrapolation is done by a new method of holding the closest preburst ratio constant. Previous methods of extrapolating prebursts < 60 minutes are still supported for legacy reasons, however the new method is the default. Similarly, preburst depths for events outside the AEP range are extrapolated using the new method of holding the closest preburst ratio constant. The legacy tool did not extrapolate for these events and the initial losses were set to zero. There is no option to go back to this method.

    Note

    Preburst depths now go down to 30 minutes, therefore extrapolation only applies for durations < 30 minutes (not 60 minutes like the legacy Data Hub)

  • The climate change options to configure ΔT or modify the baseline temperature have been removed.

  • By default, the tool will now automatically switch to using a complete storm if the preburst rainfall depth is greater than the storm initial loss (only for those specific events), however this can also be turned off.
  • The Use event independent continuing loss option has been removed as some regions use AEP specific losses.
  • The data folder has been renamed working_data and the outputs have been changed. Among other changes, plots are no longer included and the tool uses the json response format when downloading data (the legacy tool used the txt format). The json format is more code friendly to parse (unfortunately less human readable than the text format).
  • The tool no longer writes out a log file. The configuration is saved as generaged_input_<site_name>.json and messages are logged to a dedicated log widget in the dock window.

docs.title: Preburst Percentile
docs.text:
This option sets the preburst percentile to derive the preburst depths from.

The preburst depths are used in both complete storms and design burst only events.

  • complete storm: used for the rainfall depth in the preburst pattern
  • design burst only storms: used to calculate the burst initial loss: \(IL_{burst} = IL_{storm} - PB_{depth}\)

The "recommended" option will use the recommended preburst percentile(s) from the ARR Data Hub if they are provided, otherwise it will fallback to using the 50th percentile.

For example, catchments in NSW may receive a recommended preburst table from the Data Hub (which mixes 50th and 75th percentiles). However, many regions won't receive a recommended preburst table, and the 50th percentile will be used.

The "recommended" preburst will not always be the jurisdiction recommended prebursts

When the Data Hub does not provide a "recommended" preburst table, the tool falls back to the 50th percentile.

The fallback is always the 50th percentile and is not guaranteed to be the recommended percentile for any given jurisdiction. The 50th percentile is a reasonable fallback for most regions, however it is up to the user to choose an appropriate value for the given jurisdiction.

docs.title: Complete Storms
docs.text:
A complete storm prepends a preburst rainfall period ahead of the ARR design burst, so the full storm initial loss can be used rather than a burst initial loss.

Distinction between Storm and Burst Initial Loss(Source: ARR Book 5, Chapter 3, Figure 5.3.5)

The tool will automatically switch to using a complete storm for events where \(PB_{depth} > IL_{storm}\) (i.e. the burst initial loss is calculated to be less than zero).

This is triggered for individual events i.e. if a complete storm is triggered for the 1% AEP 60 min event, this will not trigger complete storms for other events if they are not required.

  • Complete storm: checking this box will force complete storms for every event. If unchecked, complete storms will trigger automatically for events that require it (unless the preburst pattern method is "None" - see next point below).
  • Complete storms can be turned off completely (no automatic switching) by setting the Preburst pattern method to "None".

docs.title: Preburst Pattern Methods
docs.text:
• Recommended:

    The "recommended" method will use the provided preburst temporal pattern if one is provided by the Data Hub. If the Data Hub does not provide preburst temporal patterns, then the recommended method will fallback to the Temporal Pattern Method (see below).

    The "recommended" method may not always be appropriate

    If the Data Hub does not provide preburst temporal patterns, the fallback method is to the use the Temporal Pattern Method.

    The ARR guideline does not make any specific recommendations on how to formulate preburst temporal patterns, as such the chosen fallback method in the tool is not something that is explicitly recommended in the guideline.

    It is up to the user to determine what an appropriate method is for their location, particularly if the Data Hub does not provide preburst temporal pattern data.

  • Constant:

    The "Constant" method applies the preburst rainfall depth equally, at a constant rate, over a given time period. See the Preburst Duration section for more information on how to set the preburst duration.

  • Temporal pattern:

    The "Temporal pattern" method uses a point temporal pattern from the burst temporal pattern data downloaded from the Data Hub. The rarity band of the preburst temporal pattern will match the burst event rarity.

    • Temporal pattern: The user can select which temporal pattern number to use for the preburst. Selecting "Design burst" will use the same temporal number as the design burst temporal pattern.

    See the Preburst Duration section below for more information on how to set the preburst duration.

  • None:

    The "None" method turns off complete storms entirely. The burst initial loss will be set to zero in instances where the complete storm would have been triggered normally.

docs.title: Preburst Duration
docs.text:
If the Preburst temporal pattern method is set to either the "Constant" or "Temporal Pattern" method, the preburst duration is determined by either:

  • Setting the Preburst duration (hrs) - this will be applied to all events, regardless of the burst duration

  • Using Proportional duration - this sets the preburst duration to be proportional to the burst duration.

    A maximum preburst duration is also in effect and can be changed by the user. This prevents long events (> 72 hrs) from blowing out due to long preburst durations.

    When using the Temporal Pattern Method, the closest temporal pattern duration is used (rounded up if equidistance between durations).

docs.title: Negligible Preburst Assumption
docs.text: If the resulting preburst depth turns out to be less than 1% of the point design burst depth (implied preburst ratio < 0.01), the preburst period is dropped entirely and the event falls back to a standard burst-only event.

docs.title: Requested Durations between a "Use PB TP" Cell and a Fixed-value Cell
docs.text:
If a requested duration falls between two rows of the burst initial loss table where one is numeric and the other is the "Use PB TP" placeholder (only applicable when the preburst temporal patterns are provided by the Data Hub), a straight linear interpolation between them wouldn't make sense (a placeholder isn't a loss value).

Instead, the tool calculates the burst initial loss, using (interpolated) preburst depths and storm initial loss. If the result is positive, it's used directly (no complete storm needed); if it is negative, the cell is treated as "Use PB TP", automatically triggering complete storm assembly for that specific AEP/duration. A duration bracketed by two "Use PB TP" cells is likewise treated as "Use PB TP" (no numeric neighbour exists to derive anything from).

docs.title: PyTUFLOW Integration
docs.text:
Under the hood, the ARR to TUFLOW tool uses PyTUFLOW to fetch and process data from the ARR Data Hub. It's possible to take the configuration file(s) saved by the ARR to TUFLOW tool and run them directly in PyTUFLOW.

In many ways, doing repeat runs is quicker to do in PyTUFLOW as it does not require opening QGIS, opening the tool, and configuring the options in the dock window. With PyTUFLOW, the configuration file(s) can be run using a single Command Line Interface (CLI) command.

pytuflow-arr config.json [config2.json ...]

See the PyTUFLOW documentation for more information: docs.tuflow.com/pytuflow/1.3/cli/pytuflow-arr.

The inverse is also true, it is possible to take a configuration file that was previously run through PyTUFLOW, and load the configuration into the ARR to TUFLOW tool. The configuration can be viewed, edited, and saved within the ARR to TUFLOW docking window - see Saving Configurations.

docs.title: PyTUFLOW Version
docs.text:
The PyTUFLOW version used to generate the outputs are written into the rf_inflow/*.csv file header:

It is recommended to keep this information (or record it elsewhere) so that the same outputs can be regenerated in future if needed.

Running on a specific version of PyTUFLOW is easily done in Python by installing the required version:

python -m pip install pytuflow==1.3.0

Running the correct version of the plugin is also quite easy, however requires matching up plugin versions with PyTUFLOW versions. This can be done by looking in the Changelog. Each time the PyTUFLOW version is changed, this will be noted in the changelog:

If the PyTUFLOW version is not noted, this means that the version was not changed from the previous version of the plugin.

Previous versions of the TUFLOW plugin can be downloaded from the following page: plugins.qgis.org/plugins/tuflow

Note, that old versions of the TUFLOW plugin may not be forward compatible with newer versions of QGIS.

docs.title: Required Settings
docs.text: The required settings tab of the tool contains all mandatory inputs for the tool to run. Unless listed as (Optional), the parameters on this tab are required.

docs.title: Inputs
docs.text:
The input catchments are specified in a table with one row per catchment. Rows can be added, removed or cleared using the add , remove and clear buttons above the table.

Each row has:

  • Name the catchment/site name. This is used to name the tools output files.

  • Catchment Method the method for defining the Catchment Location. Either:

    • GIS Layer: select the polygon layer and the specific feature from the comboboxes.

    • Latitude/Longitude: manually enter a latitude and longitude which represent the centre of the catchment.

To avoid having to populate the table one row at a time, there is an option to add multiple rows at once from a GIS polygon layer. Specify the polygon layer and the field to use as the catchment identifier and then click the button. This will add one row per feature to the table. The catchments will be named using the values from the identifying field.

For example, in the image below, the GIS polygon layer example_catchment_001_R has the identifying field Name which contains FC04, FC05, etc.

docs.title: Outlet Location (Optional)
docs.text:
Providing an outlet location is an optional input to the ARR Data Hub since the 2026 v1 update. An outlet location is only used for jurisdiction-sensitive layers (IFD, storm losses, preburst, ARF). The outlet location can be provided from a GIS point layer or by inputing the location as long/lat coordinates.

To specify an outlet location, check on the Specify catchment outlet location checkbox and then choose the Outlet location method from the combobox:

  • GIS point layer: Specify the outlet location by selecting a GIS point layer and the specific Outlet point feature from the comboboxes. The outlet point feature can also be selected from the map using the 'select point feature' tool .
  • Latitude/longitude: Specify the outlet location manually by entering the Outlet latitude and Outlet longitude.

Outlet location is global

The outlet location setting applies to every catchment in the catchments table, it is not set on a per-catchment basis.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Specify the location and format for the files output by this tool.

  • Output format The file format used for the rainfall hyetograph files, either CSV or ts1.

  • Output location The location where the output files will be written to.

docs.title: Intensity Frequency Duration (IFD)
docs.text:
• IFD baseline year: the rainfall baseline year to use for the design rainfall depths.

    • 2030 (default): uses the current climate baseline.

    • 1990 (historical): uses the historical baseline.

docs.title: Event Selection
docs.text:
Select the storm event combinations. At least one AEP and one duration must be selected for the tool to run.

  • AEP's select the Annual Exceedance Probability (AEP) events to run.

  • Durations select the storm durations to run.

Output configuration JSON uses minutes

The output configuration .json file (see Saving Configurations) uses minutes for all duration events.

Frequent events are not available

The ARR to TUFLOW tool does not scrape the BOM website for IFD information. It relies solely on the ARR Data Hub. The data hub does not currently provide IFD data for frequent events, therefore the tool does not currently support frequent events.

docs.title: Loading and Saving Configurations
docs.text:
The tool window's current settings can be saved to a configuration .json file or files (for multiple catchments), and previously saved configuration .json file(s) can be loaded back into the dock.

These configuration files are in the same format used by PyTUFLOW - see PyTUFLOW Integration.

docs.title: Loading Configurations
docs.text:
One or more configuration .json files can be loaded into the tool using the button at the top of the tool window. When clicked, a file dialog will open to select the file(s). The following behaviour differs depending on whether one file or multiple files are selected:

  • For one file, it will be loaded in directly and the tool window will be populated with its settings.
  • For multiple files, it will read the files and attempt to determine which one is the 'main' configuration. The 'main' configuration file will contain more then just the site information. If more then one file is deemed to be a 'main' configuration, a popup dialog will appear where the user can choose which one to use. If no files appear to be 'main', it will default to the first one. The 'main' file will be used to populate all settings in the tool window, apart from the catchment table. The catchment table will be populated with the site section of all the input files.

For both options, the tool will attempt to load in the catchment GIS layer(s), if provided.

Once a configuration is loaded, the tool will be populated with all settings contained in the file(s). Any options that are not set in the configuration file(s) will be left as their default in the tool window. The user can then edit and change the inputs as required (see section below for saving the changes). To reset the tool window to the loaded configuration, use the Reload dock from JSON button. This will reset all the settings in all the tabs. There are also individual reload buttons for each tab. When clicked, they reload only that tab. An example Reload 'ARF' from JSON button is shown in the image below.

Note

Loading a configuration file, or clicking any of the reload buttons will first clear the tool window (or tab, for tab-specific reload buttons) and then repopulate.

docs.title: Saving Configurations
docs.text:
The tool window's current state can be saved as a configuration file or files (for multiple catchments). This is done by clicking the Save to disk... button at the top of the tool window. When clicked, a dialog will appear with further options for customising the save, depending on the number of catchments currently configured in the tool window:

  • For one catchment, the following dialog will appear. The user can input an Output location and Filename, using the file browser if needed.

    Note that if a configuration file was loaded in, the fields will be automatically populated with its location and filename. These can be adjusted as needed.

  • For multiple catchments, the following dialog will appear. The user can select a folder for the Output location and then specify an output Filename. By default, each catchment's name will be appended to Filename before saving. However, placeholders ${name} and/or ${enum} are available to customise the output filename. ${name} will be replaced with the catchment name and ${enum} with a number corresponding to the catchments position in the input table. For example, config-SEQ-${name}-${enum}.json may have an output name like config-SEQ-SubCatchment_A-1.json.

    Note that if a configuration file was loaded in, the Output location and Filename will be automatically populated with its location and filename.

docs.title: Temporal Patterns
docs.text:
The temporal pattern options allow the user to add additional temporal patterns to the rainfall boundary outputs. Temporal patterns can be added by extracting patterns from other regions, or from using unused temporal patterns from within the same region.

Adding temporal pattern options will stack

Adding temporal patterns from both the same and different regions will stack.

For example, selecting an additional region + using all point temporal patterns will result in 60 point temporal patterns per event.

\[ 10\ \text{temporal patterns} \times 2\ \text{regions} \times 3\ \text{rarity bands} = 60 \]

docs.title: Additional Temporal Pattern - Adding Regions
docs.text: Additional temporal patterns can be added from different regions by selecting region(s) in the box. These are additional regions that will be added to the output i.e. it is not required to select the region the catchment location falls within, this will automatically be included.

docs.title: Additional Temporal Patterns - Same Region
docs.text:
Additional temporal patterns can be added from the same region:

  • Use additional point temporal patterns available within region

    Checking this option will add 20 extra point temporal patterns. The extra temporal patterns are taken from the unused rarity bands for any given event.

    For example, if a 1% AEP event is selected, usually this would output 10 "rare" point temporal patterns.

    If this option is checked, the "frequent" and "intermediate" temporal patterns will also be included, resulting in 30 temporal patterns in total.

  • Use additional areal temporal patterns

    If checked on, additional areal temporal patterns from the next closest area band will be added based on the number set in the input. If the input is 1, then an additional 10 temporal patterns will be added. A value of 2 will add 20 temporal patterns, and so on (up to 8).

    For example, if the catchment is 100 km2, the base areal temporal patterns would use the Area 100 areal temporal pattern band. If this option is checked on and the input value is set to 1, then the output will also include the Area 200 areal temporal pattern band. If the value is set to 2 then both the Area 200 and Area 500 temporal pattern bands will be added (resulting in 30 temporal patterns in total).

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Additional temporal patterns will be added the appropriate event CSV output in the rf_inflow folder.

The relevant information will be added as a suffix to the colum names in the rf_inflow/*.csv outputs. This includes to the base temporal pattern set.

Example 1: Column names after adding an additional temporal pattern region Example 2: Column names after adding all point temporal patterns

docs.title: Use Previously Downloaded ARR Data
docs.text:
The tool can pass in data that has already been downloaded from the ARR Data Hub. This can be useful when re-running a prior catchment/configuration to re-generate outputs. For example, when modifying the configuration to use new methods, but retain consistency with previous outputs.

Some features cannot be added to a prior run

Some features of the tool cannot be added to a previously downloaded response from the data hub. For example, climate change settings will affect what the tool requests from the data hub. Therefore, it is not possible to add climate change to a prior download that did not include it, since the response json won't contain the relevant information.

It might also be a requirement to run the same version of the tool to ensure completely identical outputs. See the PyTUFLOW page for information on how to accomplish that.

docs.title: ARR Data Hub Response JSON
docs.text:
A previously saved ARR Data Hub response .json file can be loaded via the ARR Data Hub response JSON file.

Response vs Configuration JSON files

The response JSON file is not the same as the configuration JSON file.

The response JSON is the file/format provided by the ARR Data Hub when information is requested and contains most of the relevant data from the datahub in its raw form (temporal pattern data is downloaded separately as CSV files).

The configuration JSON is a TUFLOW Plugin/PyTUFLOW specific format that contains the parameters for the tool.

If a response file is set, the tool will use the data contained within it instead of making a new query to the data hub.

Temporal pattern data (in CSV format) is downloaded separately to the response JSON. The temporal pattern data will still be downloaded from the data hub unless previously downloaded temporal pattern files are also provided (see Manually Specified Temporal Patterns below). If the response JSON and temporal pattern CSVs are provided, then the tool will run completely offline.

Note

The response .json file is specific to a single catchment/outlet location, so this option is only intended to be used when there is a single row in the catchments table.

docs.title: Manually Specified Temporal Patterns
docs.text:
Previously downloaded point and areal temporal patterns can also be manually specified via .csv files. These must be in the same format that the datahub provides them.

  • Point: path to a point temporal pattern .csv file.

  • Areal: path to an areal temporal pattern .csv file.

docs.title: Loading
docs.text:
The bc tables check can be loaded by loading any of the following GIS check files in QGIS:

  • _1d_bc_check
  • _bcc_check
  • _sac_check

Loading any one of the above GIS files into QGIS will automatically load data from the "_bc_tables_check.csv" file for plotting purposes. These files are all standard GIS files that can be loaded into QGIS in the standard way.

The data from the "_bc_tables_check.csv" file is only initially partially loaded and only completely loaded when trying to plot from the file for the first time. This is so the initial loading of the GIS file is fast and only loads the tabular data if it is needed for plotting. This also means that the first time any plotting is done, it may take a little longer than subsequent plots, as the data from the "_bc_tables_check.csv" file is being loaded for the first time.

The tabular data from the "_bc_tables_check.csv" file is linked to the GIS layers and will be closed when the GIS layers are closed.

docs.title: Plotting
docs.text:
The BC tables check format is supported in the following plot types:

  • Time Series Plot

The BC tables check format only supports plotting using the selection tool. See the Plot Window documentation for more information on plotting.

Only unique IDs will be plotted from the BC tables check format. This means that it is OK to select multiple features along the same boundary and TUFLOW Viewer will only plot a single time series for that boundary.

Example: Plotting the QT time series and HQ curve from a bcc_check file

docs.title: TUFLOW Viewer V2 vs Legacy TUFLOW Viewer
docs.text:
The first, and main, difference between the legacy TUFLOW Viewer and the new TUFLOW Viewer is the removal of the docking widget interface. The new viewer has no interface and instead relies on native functionality within QGIS to provide a more integrated experience. This means there is no longer a dedicated time slider provided by TUFLOW Viewer and the user should use the QGIS Temporal Controller to adjust the output timestep.

QGIS Temporal Controller

Likewise, when selecting the active result types, the QGIS layer properties should be used to adjust which data type is active for mesh based results. It is recommended to use the Styling Panel rather than the properties dialogue, as this can be toggled quickly with the F7 or Ctrl+3 keyboard shortcuts and does not lock the interface with a modal dialogue.

QGIS Styling Panel

Note, the new TUFLOW Viewer removes the interface, but is still working in the background to provide a better experience when working with TUFLOW results in QGIS. As an example, the TUFLOW Viewer enables XMDF files to be opened in QGIS by dragging and dropping them directly from Windows File Explorer. It also allows results to be dragged from one QGIS instance to another.

docs.title: High Level Differences
docs.text:
1. Removal of the docking widget interface as mentioned above.

  2. The new viewer is built on top of the PyTUFLOW Python library which provides a more robust and efficient method for reading TUFLOW results. Users should notice an improved performance all round, especially when loading and plotting from large ESTRY result files. Load times of large XMDF files are similar between the legacy and new viewer as this is controlled by the underlying QGIS library. Although a significant performance improvement has been made to the section plot, see the table below for more detailed metrics. Along with the section plot performance improvement, PyTUFLOW will perform better caching of data in the background, so users should still notice an improvement here too when replotting previously plotted locations (e.g. when scrolling backwards and forward through timesteps on a section plot).

    Section plot performance comparison between legacy TUFLOW Viewer and TUFLOW Viewer V2. Model Name Number of Cells Selected by Line Legacy TUFLOW Viewer (sec) TUFLOW Viewer V2 (sec)** FMA_T2_10.00m 1,205 28.0 0.76 FMA_T2_05.00m 2,367 267 1.15 FMA_T2_02.50m 4,690 —* 2.99

    Note

    * Legacy TUFLOW Viewer was unable to complete the section plot within a reasonable timeframe (> 30 minutes).

    ** The majority of the time is taken finding the intersecting cells along the line, subsequent data extraction is significantly faster.

  3. Each loaded result is tied directly to a specific GIS layer, or set of GIS layers. For example, an XMDF is linked to the mesh layer, and the TPC result is tied to the "_PLOT_" layers that are loaded when the TPC file is opened. Once those layers are removed from QGIS, the results are also unloaded, this means that they will no longer be available for plotting. The biggest affect that this might have is when loading multiple TPC results which will load in multiple sets of "_PLOT_" layers. The plot layers may be identical (e.g. when loading in results from different events), however the user must keep all the layers in QGIS to keep the results available for plotting. It is still possible to plot the different results by selecting a channel from a single "_PLOT_" layer, as long as the ID is present in the other TPC results.

docs.title: Specific Differences
docs.text: This section is designed to give a brief overview of some of the more specific differences between the legacy and new viewer for users who are familiar with the legacy TUFLOW Viewer. It is not an exhaustive list, but covers some of the more notable changes so users can get started quickly without reading through the entire user guide.

docs.title: Plotting
docs.text:
1. Map output - plot "from map multi": In the legacy TUFLOW Viewer, there was a specific plotting option to add multiple points, or multiple lines, to a single-plot. This is now inherently supported by the "Draw Tool" without any special options required. Each time the user clicks on the map, a new point is added to the plot (or a similar experience with lines when plotting sections). These locations can be redrawn by holding down Ctrl and clicking on the map again. Locations can also be individually toggled or removed via the "Draw Tool" menu.
  2. Map output - plot from "layer selection": This option can be found under the "Selection Tool" menu as Extract from map outputs.
  3. Time-series - selecting channels: The "Selection Tool" must be active before selecting any times-series features to plot from. This has the benefit being able to be toggled off and then the QGIS selection tool can be used for other tasks without interfering with what is being plotted.
  4. Time-series plot - show current time: This option can be found under the time-series plot context menu. The vertical time indicator line is also interactable and can be dragged to change the current time.
  5. Time-series plot - use datetime: This option can be found under the time series plot context menu.
  6. Secondary axis: Plot items can be moved to the secondary axis by right-clicking the item on the plot and selecting Move to secondary axis. They can be moved back to the primary axis in the same way. This works a little differently from the legacy behaviour where the entire result type was moved to the secondary axis. It is now done by specific plot item, so velocity from one location can be on the primary axis, while velocity from another location can be on the secondary axis.
  7. Plot navigation: Plot navigation (pan and zoom) is always active in the new TUFLOW Viewer. Use the left mouse button (or middle mouse button) to pan the plot, use the right mouse button to scale the plot, and use the mouse wheel to zoom. For secondary axes, hold down Shift or Ctrl to pan/zoom the secondary axis. Alternatively for secondary axes, the user can interact with the axis ticks directly to pan/zoom the secondary axis (e.g. left click and drag on the axis ticks on the right-hand side to pan the secondary axis up and down).
  8. Freezing the axis limits: If the plot axes are changed by the user (e.g. panning or zooming), the axes will remain fixed to those limits. The auto limit behaviour can be restored by clicking auto button in the bottom left of the plot window. Plot limits can also be manually set by right-clicking the plot window and looking under the X axis or Y axis sub-menus (not available for the secondary axis yet).
  9. Exporting data: The export and copy data options are now found under the plot context menu.

docs.title: Styling
docs.text: 1. Mesh - saving default style: In the legacy TUFLOW Viewer, it was possible to save the current style to be the default style for the given result type. This is still possible and can be found by right-clicking the mesh layer in the QGIS Layers Panel and selecting the TUFLOW Viewer submenu. The style is cached into a local folder and unlike the legacy viewer, will survive plugin updates.

docs.title: Loading
docs.text:
Flood Modeller cross-sections and results can be loaded either via the .dat or .gxy files. They can be loaded by dragging the file into the QGIS Map Canvas from a file explorer or from the Browser Panel. If loading via the .gxy, a dialogue will appear and prompt the user to select optional .dat and result files.

Additional notes on loading from either the .dat or .gxy file:

  • Loading via the .dat file, any given cross-section must contain eastings and northings to load into QGIS.
  • Loading via the .dat file will load only the cross-sections and not any results.
  • Loading via the .gxy file, it is not required to include a .dat file or any results.
  • Results can be a single .zzn, or multiple CSV files exported from Flood Modeller or from the Python API.
  • If a .dat file is not included, some result types will not be available in the Section Plot, such as "bed level" and "pipes".
  • Long sections will favour the .dat file if it is available. Long sections generated with a .dat compared with only the .gxy file may differ. This is due to potential differences in connectivity and channel lengths.

docs.title: Reference Time
docs.text:
The reference time determines the isodate values shown for the "Animation Range" in the Temporal Controller window. Typically, if loading results from a .zzn, a reference time will be included in the result. Otherwise, if loading results from a CSV, there will not be a reference time.

If the Flood Modeller result does not have an inherent reference time, the following hierarchy is used to set the reference time:

  • If a result with an inherent reference time is added to the workspace, or exists in the workspace already, then the reference time of the Flood Modeller results will be updated to match the other reference time.
  • Given no other source, TUFLOW Viewer will default to '1990-01-01 00:00:00'.

There is currently no method of changing the reference time of the Flood Modeller result within QGIS.

docs.title: Plotting
docs.text:
The Flood Modeller result format is supported in the following plot types:

  • Time Series Plot
  • Section Plot

The Flood Modeller result only supports plotting using the selection tool. See the Plot Window documentation for more information on plotting. Note: Flood Modeller results are contained on nodes and not links, so the user should select nodes when plotting.

Within the Section Plot, the generated long sections can be limited to a section of channels by selecting an upstream and downstream node. It is also possible to select more than two nodes, as long as one of the selected nodes is downstream of all the other selected nodes (this will be treated as multiple branches).

Note: It is not yet possible to plot water level results on the cross-sections.

Example: Plotting the flow time series in a channel from Flood Modeller results Example: Plotting cross-sections and long sections from Flood Modeller results
